That number is the slope of one tangent line. But a curve has many points, and the slope usually changes from point to point. If the point moves, the derivative moves with it.
So the derivative is not only a number. It is also a new function.

paragraphs.title: Leibniz notation remembers the units
paragraphs.p: If s(t) is position in meters and t is time in seconds, then \frac{ds}{dt} has units meters/seconds. So
If T(t) is temperature in degrees Celsius and t is time in minutes, then \frac{dT}{dt} has units ^\circ\text{C}/\text{minute}. So \dfrac{dT}{dt} measures how quickly the temperature is changing.

statement.p: The notation \frac{dy}{dx} comes from the quotient \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}. At this stage, it means a limit of such quotients. It is not introduced as an ordinary fraction of two real numbers.
In the next section, dx and dy will acquire a useful meaning through linear approximation.

subsection.title: Reading f' from the graph of f
subsection.p: The graph of f contains the graph of f' in hidden form. At each x, the value f'(x) is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of f.
This gives several visual rules.

table.title: Geometric features of f and their meaning for f'

statement.p: Let f(x)=x^3-3x. We compute f'(x) from the definition. The difference quotient is
The derivative graph is a graph of slopes.
The original graph has horizontal tangents at x=-1 and x=1. The derivative graph has zeros there: f'(-1)=0, f'(1)=0.
At x=0, the original graph is falling with slope -3. The derivative graph has value f'(0)=-3.
The derivative graph does not show the height of f. It shows how the height is changing.

subsection.title: Reading f from the graph of f'
subsection.p: The derivative graph also gives information in the opposite direction.
If f'(x)\gt 0, then the tangent slopes are positive, so f is rising.
If f'(x)\lt 0, then the tangent slopes are negative, so f is falling.
If f'(x)=0, then the graph of f has a horizontal tangent.
For the example f'(x)=3x^2-3, we have 3x^2-3\gt 0 when x\lt -1 or x\gt 1. So the graph of f is rising on those intervals.
We also have 3x^2-3\lt 0 when -1\lt x\lt 1. So the graph of f is falling there.
Thus the derivative graph tells the shape story:
This is why derivatives help us understand graphs. A derivative is local information, but when we collect it point by point, it begins to describe the whole curve.

paragraphs.title: What f' does not tell by itself
paragraphs.p: The derivative does not remember vertical shifts.
The two graphs have the same slopes at corresponding x-values, but one graph is 5 units higher.

statement.p: A derivative records change. Adding a constant changes height, but not slope.

paragraphs.p: This points toward the second half of calculus. If we know all the slopes f'(x), how much of f can we recover? We will eventually need a starting value and a way to accumulate slope information.
Before that larger question, we use the derivative for a more local purpose: near one point, a curve can be replaced by a line.
